scenes.title: Cold open
narration: The Eagle's Flight: Sumazau
This is Sumazau. Traditional.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The Sumazau originates from the Kadazan-Dusun and Murut peoples of Sabah, Malaysia, with deep roots in agricultural and ritual life.

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Performed for the Kaamatan harvest festival, weddings, and rituals like the magang (post-headhunting) and moginum.
Today it is a living tradition.

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Dancers move in pairs, shifting weight with bent knees and swinging arms.
A male dancer cues a transition to an outstretched arm position on tiptoes, mimicking an eagle.
Watch for Eagle Flight.
on_screen: Captions name each signature move as it appears
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: The ensemble consists of the sompogogungan (six to seven hanging gongs), the gandang (a double-headed drum), and sometimes a kulintangan (gong-chime or metallophone).
Listen for the Sompogogungan (hanging gongs), Gandang (drum), Kulintangan (metallophone).
A steady, interlocking percussive sound dominated by the deep resonance of hanging gongs and the rhythmic beat of a double-headed drum.
on_screen: Instrument names on screen as each is mentioned
Waveform or rhythm-pattern graphic: Interlocking parts starting with the gandang, followed by the sompogogungan.

scenes.title: The costume and the setting
narration: Dancers wear the sinombiaka (black cloth with gold braid).
Women wear tangkong (brass rings) and himpogot (coin belts); men wear the sigar (headcloth).

narration: Norbert Andilah (viral PPE dancer), Tunku Azizah Aminah Maimunah Iskandariah (Queen consort of Malaysia).
Magarang (Liwan Dusun), Sumayau (Lotud Dusun), Mongigol (Tindal Dusun), Mongigol Sumundai (Rungus), Mangalai (Tinagas Dusun).
Indigenous Sabah traditions of the Kadazan-Dusun and Murut peoples.

scenes.title: A respectful note
narration: The dance is performed in ritual contexts such as the Monogit healing ceremony and post-headhunting rites; outsiders should respect the cultural significance and ritual nature of these events.
